#5423. From Monk To Startups: One Founder’s Unusual Path To Building Government Software

Editor’s note: The following is the latest profile in a series of articles about startup founders from non-technical backgrounds who have launched successful venture-backed companies. Read the previous interviews in the series including with MagicSchool AI founder Adeel Khan here, Trunk Tools founder Sarah Buchner here, Tabs founder Ali Hussain here, Craft founder Ilya Levtov here, GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti here, Incredible Health co-founder Iman Abuzeid here, and Hilt founder William “Will” Cielen here.

Lilly Chen was 16 and had been repeatedly hospitalized for Graves’ disease when her mother suggested they move to China and become monks. Frustrated with the care her daughter was receiving through Medicaid, she wanted to try something different.

Chen left high school and spent about two years as a monk, ordained in the United States before spending several months at a monastery in China. She meditated, reread the same books, and gradually felt well enough to consider returning to school.

She went on to enter Colorado College without a high school diploma, briefly play video games professionally, and become an engineer at Facebook. When she quit that job, she didn’t have a startup idea. She just wanted to find work she believed in.

That mission eventually led her to FSH (pronounced “fish) Technologies,” a Philadelphia-based company that’s building software for some of the government’s least glamorous tasks, including administering school food services and managing public records.

After her brief stint at a large tech company, Chen realized she wanted to tackle the everyday problems that make people’s lives harder, even if solving them wouldn’t generate much excitement in Silicon Valley.

“What does it actually take to solve the really unsexy, boring stuff?” she remembers asking herself.

Before Chen was thinking about government software, she was trying to get well enough to return to school.

At the monastery in China, she meditated, ate food grown on-site or brought by nearby villagers, and lived without internet access. She continued taking thyroid medication and said her health became more manageable during that period.

She also read. A lot. With no nearby place to buy books, she reread the ones she had brought, finding different places around the monastery to sit with them.

Her attachment to those books prompted a conversation with a fellow monk who asked what she enjoyed about reading and where she might find more books. The discussion eventually turned to colleges, and why she wasn’t attending one.

Chen explained her health problems. He observed that she seemed well. She realized she was.

So Chen returned to the U.S., homeschooled herself and enrolled at Colorado College without having earned a high school diploma. She turned 20 during her freshman year and graduated in 2019 with a double major in mathematics and economics.

While she was in college, Chen briefly played Dota 2 professionally. She also played against OpenAI’s game-playing bots, an early encounter with AI technology she would later help support as an engineer.

After an initial job in Boston, she joined Facebook, where she built infrastructure used to train AI models.

Then on Jan. 6, 2021, Chen was attending a remote company all-hands meeting while watching coverage of the attack on the U.S. Capitol on another screen. Her concerns about Facebook’s role in enabling the organization of violence made her question whether she could continue working there.

“I realized that I couldn’t work for Big Tech anymore,” she recalls.

To figure out her next move, she returned to the sort of questions she had encountered as a monk. What made her happy? What mattered to her? What was she good at?

Programming remained her most concrete skill. She just needed to figure out where to apply it.

An introduction through Envision, a student-run accelerator focused on nontraditional founders, connected her with Contrary, a venture firm that has backed the likes of Ramp and Anduril Industries. The firm wrote Chen her first check in 2021, before she had even settled on the business that would become FSH.

Although she didn’t have a developed company pitch, Chen’s earnest explanation of what motivated her and her passion for solving a meaningful problem won investors over. That investment gave her room to experiment, she said.

FSH took shape into what it is today in 2024. The Contrary investor who first backed her, Jason Chen, has since joined the company as its chief operating officer.

The company has raised $25 million in total funding, including a recent $20 million Series A that Chen said came together in about a week. Participants in that raise included Lachy Groom, General Catalyst, Ramp, Scribble Ventures, Operator Partners, Basis Set Ventures. Contrary also led its seed financing.

Ultimately, Chen landed on government software because in her view, it had the potential to solve many consequential problems that attracted relatively little excitement.

For example, permits, licenses, grant applications and other administrative processes can be slow for reasons that extend beyond an outdated interface, Chen noted. Information may exist in separate departments. Updating a website may require approvals from multiple stakeholders including policymakers, communications staff and an IT team.

Putting a chatbot on top of that system, Chen argues, leaves much of the underlying problem unresolved.

Her approach to solving some of the problems that exist within governments draws on an exchange she had years earlier at the monastery, where one of her chores was feeding koi.

The head monk would periodically ask her if she thought she was the fish or the pond?

Initially, Chen didn’t understand what he was asking. But he kept returning to the question, and she began thinking about it. Eventually, she picked a fish she thought resembled her: one that stayed out of fights, swam with the group and occasionally ventured off on its own.

The head monk’s response was, “You’re the pond, not the fish.”

Chen viewed the exchange as a lesson in looking beyond individual pieces to understand how a whole system works. Looking at government software, she believed that it meant examining why information is scattered or processes are slow before deciding what technology to build.

One early area for FSH has been K-12 food services, where administrators must perform tasks such as coordinating meal planning, nutritional information and reimbursement requirements. Another is records and archive management, including the paper documents that can still require residents to visit a government office to retrieve them.

FSH does use AI for tasks such as optical character recognition, translation and natural-language search. But, Chen said, the company treats it as a tool within its software, rather than relying on a chatbot or an AI agent to handle an entire process.

Government sales have required patience. The company generated less than $100,000 in revenue in its first year, Chen said, reflecting the time it takes to win contracts. At the time of this interview, FSH had roughly eight or nine employees, with additional offers outstanding.

Chen’s time as a monk has also influenced how she runs the company.

She admits she is skeptical of startup culture that treats sleeping in the office or working extremely long hours as evidence of commitment or a badge of pride. Rather, Chen views some of that behavior as performative, especially when it comes at the expense of the rest that she believes people need to work effectively.

Her preferred motto to the team is, “Slow is smooth and smooth is fast.”

“We think slowly about a lot of things, and then we do things quickly,” she said.

Chen believes it’s crucial to first understand the people, departments and procedures behind a government service before trying to improve it.

Looking back, Chen also credits her success to finding people willing to back someone whose experience didn’t resemble the usual résumé. That includes the college that admitted her without a high school diploma and an investor who wrote a check before she had settled on a company idea.

“You definitely end up finding your own way if you just stick to being weird,” she said.

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

Solana is under fresh pressure after falling below the important $107 support level. Analysts have pointed to heavy ETF outflows and plummeting spot trading volume as the latest developments pushing the market back into a defensive phase.

SOL is currently caught between a rock and a hard place, hovering around $95 on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. The price has fallen 5.81% over the past week as short-term weakness battles a longer-term recovery. The asset is facing pressure to move above the crucial $107 support zone. Analysts believe this could decide whether the market falls further or renew its recovery.

The asset is facing massive liquidity pressure as persistent outflows from spot ETFs create sustained downward pressure on the fifth-largest cryptocurrency. Recent analysis from analyst Sovereign Yield shows Solana is trapped below its critical support region of $107, suggesting potential volatility ahead for SOL investors.

Persistent ETF outflows signal that institutional demand for SOL has weakened significantly in October, according to data from Sovereign Yield. Meanwhile, a report from CryptoQuant analysts indicates further difficulties in the Solana market. According to the CryptoQuant data, spot Solana trading volume shows a bearish shift, as spot selling volume has surpassed spot buying volume for the first time in more than six months. This trend reversal signals a shift in market sentiment.

According to the data, Solana’s spot volume bubble map signals weakening buying interest, rising investor caution, and more common risk-off positioning in the market.

The two key metrics above (from Sovereign Yield and CryptoQuant analysts) show that demand for Solana ETFs and spot selling has weakened in recent weeks. This indicates lower investor confidence.

Bearish signals have risen sharply, rising concerns about a greater correction. If selling pressure continues, the analysts believe Solana could drop below the $100 level soon.

#5420. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5419. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

#5418. The Invisible Graph: How Companies Grow Revenue And Still Lose Value

I got off the phone with a potential client whose company is doing great. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit.

The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls.

Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing.

Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%.

These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit.

The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers.

Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow.

Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken.

Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes.

A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts.

Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change.

Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance.

However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph.

#5415. Exclusive: Numeracle Raises $28M To Keep Legitimate Business Calls From Spam Label

Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels.

The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation.

The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected.

Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents.

Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers.

For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning.

Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone.

Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West, said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016.

She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling.

About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen.

“Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking.

Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle.

She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes.

“When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said.

That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A.

Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare.

The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers.

Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls.

Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers.

Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam.

AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles.

“The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.”

She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail.

Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort.

The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call.

For Lenard Marcus, a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers.

He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.”

Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales.

Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said.

“She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added.

Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent.

“This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said.

#5412. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?

#5411. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

Tech Layoffs Continue In A Week Led By EBay And Electronic Arts

Nearly a dozen tech companies reported a reduction in force in the past couple of weeks, affecting at least 1,790 workers.

The majority of this week’s tally comes from eBay, which reported its second round of 2026 layoffs. According to a report in Reuters, the San Jose, California-based e-commerce giant is trimming its workforce by 1,100, or 9%, in an effort to “simplify operations and shift resources to its fastest-growing areas.”

The gaming sector also ranked high in this week’s count with a pair of companies reporting layoffs. Leading that industry count in the disclosed number of workers affected is Redwood City, California-based Electronic Arts. Per a report in Variety, the software provider is restructuring its studios business, which includes the total shutdown of its BioWare games studio in Edmonton, Canada. Since this is a global cut, it’s unclear how many U.S. workers will be affected.

And, in a workforce reduction that hasn’t made it to the layoff stage, yet, earlier this week Microsoft said it is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 of its global employees. Per a report in Reuters, a source said the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant is making the offer available to staff company-wide, with the exception of its marketing, commercial business and security divisions.

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Oct. 28, 2026: At least 1,790 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

#5410. Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups

Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning.

U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done.

Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase. Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020.

Uncork Capital‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal.

A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic, a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed, right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures, then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later.

Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything.

The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion.

At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine.

From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside.

A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one.

#5409. Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

About 135,700 Bitcoin options worth $10.9 billion expire on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, October 30, a third of the exchange’s open contracts, two days after the Federal Reserve held rates in a 10–2 vote that left a December hike open.The price is sitting almost on top of the expiry’s pain point. BTC trades at $79,976, down 1.8% in 24 hours, after giving back its whole post-Fed bounce overnight. Max pain for Friday’s Bitcoin options expiry, the price at which buyers of those contracts would lose the most, is $78,000, and the October low that has held for a week is $79,221.

So what exactly is expiring, how did Bitcoin take the Fed, and can it hold $79,000 through Friday?

🚨 BREAKING: Bitcoin PLUNGES below $80,000 as tech stocks tumble and crypto liquidations hit $335 MILLION in 24 hours. pic.twitter.com/AZRs51zPv2

Mostly bullish bets that are now far out of reach. Deribit’s public order book data at 09:01 UTC on Thursday shows 135,676 BTC in contracts dated October 30, out of 397,442 BTC across all Deribit expiries:

Deribit BTC open interest expiring October 30, by strike. Source: Deribit

The Deribit Volatility Index (DVOL), which tracks the 30-day volatility priced into Bitcoin options, fell to 36 from 38 over the past two days. Options traders are paying less for protection even with an expiry this size a day away. Ether adds a smaller expiry of about 338,000 ETH, roughly $780 million.

Discover: BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Managed Protection ETF Would Trade Bitcoin’s Upside for a 10% Floor: Who Is It Built For?

A two-hour rally, then a slow leak. The Fed’s statement on Wednesday kept the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voting for a quarter-point hike instead. Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the next move: “I don’t believe in forward guidance, absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis.”

ETF buyers stayed in. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $137.3 million on Wednesday, their third straight day of inflows, nearly all of it into BlackRock’s IBIT, SoSoValue figures show.

A soft day after the Fed is normal for Bitcoin. On Binance data, BTC was higher 24 hours after only 33 of the Fed’s 71 decisions since January 2018, and after holds the bigger moves tended to come weeks later.

It has so far, but with less room each time. On the 4-hour chart, BTC sits at $80,130, below both its 50-period EMA at $80,978 and its 200-period EMA at $81,635. The faster line crossed under the slower one around October 23, and Wednesday’s post-Fed rally stalled right at the 200 EMA.

The floor is the October 24 low at $79,221. Bitcoin has dipped into the $79,200–$79,850 area on five of the last six days and bounced each time, most recently at 02:00 UTC on Thursday.

Max pain is only a reference point. It marks where option buyers would collect the least on Friday, and the price is under no obligation to go there.

Friday’s settlement clears a third of Deribit’s open bets in one go, and most of them were placed for a market well above $80,000. After the Bitcoin options expiry, the next tests come from data, not derivatives: the October jobs report on November 6 and consumer prices on November 10, both on the road to the Fed’s December 9 decision.

#5407. Chainlink Goes Live on Stellar, Unlocking DeFi Applications Across the $4B RWA Ecosystem

By accessing highly reliable and accurate market data through the Chainlink oracle, Stellar unlocks greater DeFi applications to meet its RWA utilities.

In a groundbreaking move to accelerate the transition to the on-chain financial ecosystem, Stellar Network today announced the integration of Chainlink into its protocol. In a blog post published today, Stellar revealed that it has adopted Chainlink’s data feeds as its official oracle solution.

Stellar Network is a decentralized blockchain network recognized for facilitating rapid, cheap, and secure cross-border payments and fund transfer applications for institutions and individuals. However, one shortcoming of traditional blockchains, like Stellar Network and several others, is their inability to access real-world data directly. Stellar aims to address this by adopting Chainlink oracles.

Chainlink oracles are specialized smart contracts that bridge blockchain networks and external data sources. They enable reliable and secure exchange of real-world data (like asset prices) to and from blockchain smart contracts. By adopting Chainlink oracles, Stellar expands the capabilities of its blockchain infrastructure, allowing it to interact with off-chain data in a trustless, decentralized manner.

Chainlink’s price feed is a crucial blockchain instrument that connects smart contracts and real-world data. Many DeFi applications across chains rely on these price feeds to keep their services running smoothly.

As a result, by adopting Chainlink’s oracle, Stellar aims to expand its protocol’s capabilities. This means that Stellar’s DeFi ecosystem now has access to reliable pricing data through Chainlink’s scale program.

The oracle integration is set to unlock a new level of DeFi adoption on Stellar. With Chainlink’s data streams and data feeds now available on Stellar, developers have access to the market data needed to build on-chain applications that connect Stellar’s advancing RWA ecosystem with DeFi.

Stellar’s blockchain already supports $4+ billion in RWAs, with assets moving on-chain. The incorporation of a Chainlink oracle ensures assets are priced, traded, used as collateral, and borrowed against reliably. With the integration, liquidity and assets on Stellar become part of a productive DeFi ecosystem where customers put their capital (e.g., tokenized stocks, stablecoins, and various assets) to work.

#5406. Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.

#5405. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5404. The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Physical AI And Predictions Lead The Lineup

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

This week featured a robust lineup of large rounds, led by manufacturing startup Re:Build, which closed on $2.1 billion, and predictions marketplace Kalshi, which picked up another $1 billion. Other sectors in which startups drew significant rounds included construction automation, biotech, batteries and enterprise AI.

1. Re:Build, $2.1B, manufacturing: Re:Build, a manufacturing startup that partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production, secured $2.1 billion in new funding. General Catalyst and JPMorganChase led the financing for the 6-year-old, Framingham, Massachusetts-based company.

2. Kalshi, $1B, predictions marketplace: Predictions marketplace Kalshi announced a $1 billion Series G financing led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital. The round set a $40 billion post-money valuation for New York-based Kalshi, which says its business’ annualized trading volume now exceeds $1 trillion.

3. Bedrock Robotics, $600M, construction tech: San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics,  a developer of autonomous systems for heavy equipment used in construction, raised $600 million in Series C funding led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital. The round brings Bedrock’s total funding to nearly $1 billion and sets a post-money valuation of $4.1 billion.

4. Dren Bio, $350M, biotech: Dren Bio, a developer of antibody therapeutics for cancer and autoimmune diseases, closed on $350 million in a new round led by Juvia Group and Lightspeed Venture Partners. The funding will support advanced trials for the San Carlos, California-based company’s blood cancer therapies.

5. Group 14 Technologies, $169M, battery tech: Woodinville, Washington-based Group 14 Technologies, a manufacturer and supplier of advanced silicon battery materials, picked up $169 million in Series D extension funding. The company also announced plans to expand into Europe with a production facility in Sagunto, Spain.

6. (tied) Firehawk Aerospace, $150M, defense tech: Firehawk Aerospace, a developer of propulsion technology, said it secured over $150 million in Series D funding at a valuation of more than $1.4 billion. Advent and Rochefort led the financing for the 7-year-old, Dallas-based company.

#5402. More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year

Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

#5399. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

The drop came in two legs. BTC opened the 20:00 UTC hour on Thursday at $80,850 and hit $78,297 within minutes as news of the Binance breach spread, a 3.2% fall. It bounced, then slid again after 23:00 UTC and printed its $76,500 low just after 02:00 UTC on Friday, 5.4% below where the hour began.

Forced selling did much of the work. CoinGlass data showed $1.55 billion of crypto positions liquidated in 24 hours, 83.6% of them longs, with $501.6 million in BTC alone.

Smaller accounts bought the dip: the share of OKX accounts that are long jumped as the price fell, and open interest rose by about $210 million into the low. Funding on OKX’s BTC perpetual stayed positive throughout, so longs are still paying shorts.

Implied volatility told a more cautious story. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility options traders are pricing in, jumped from 37 before the hack to 42 just before midnight UTC and has only eased back to 38.7.

About 135,000 BTC of options expired on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, the last Friday of the month, when monthly contracts settle. Max pain, the strike where the most options expire worthless, sat at $78,000. Deribit settled the contracts at $78,119.01.

The book was heavily tilted toward calls. Deribit data reported before the expiry put the put/call ratio at 0.53, close to two calls for every put. With BTC settling just above $78,000, most of those calls, bets that BTC would be higher by the end of October, expired worthless.

Once the expiry cleared, Deribit’s BTC options open interest stood at 285,073 BTC, or about $22.1 billion, as of 11:17 UTC.

BTC options notional by Deribit expiry as of 11:17 UTC on October 30, 2026. Source: Deribit.

Max pain isn’t a forecast; BTC often settles far from it. But the November levels frame the range traders are betting on: puts clustered at $74,000 to $76,000, right around the 200-day EMA, and calls stacked from $90,000 up.

One more sign of caution: in the 24 hours to 11:17 UTC on Friday, Deribit traders bought 1.63 BTC of puts for every BTC of calls, the reverse of the call-heavy book that just expired.

On the daily chart since early August, BTC is back where it spent most of September: between its 200-day EMA at $76,468 and its 50-day EMA at $80,593. Friday’s low wick stopped $32 above the 200-day line, which BTC has closed above every day since its late-August breakout.

August 2 to October 30, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

The levels line up with the options book:

BTC has tested this 200-day zone before. In mid-September, it dipped to $74,968, held, and ran to $87,395 within a week. Friday’s buyers are betting on the same bounce, as the OKX long/short ratio shows.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

For Bitcoin, the next test is Binance itself. If withdrawals reopen smoothly within the promised 48 hours, the call-heavy positioning that just expired worthless could rebuild toward the $90,000 strikes. If they don’t, the puts at $74,000 to $76,000 are where traders have already placed their bets.

#5396. Upwind raises $400M after walking away from Datadog acquisition offer

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Upwind, a San Francisco startup that uses AI to secure cloud infrastructure, has raised a $400 million Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from existing backers including Greylock Partners and Craft Ventures.

The round comes nine months after Upwind closed its previous $250 million financing at a $1.5 billion valuation.

The fresh funding, which has been in the works for months, nearly fell apart after Datadog attempted to buy the company, according to a person familiar with Upwind. Datadog is a publicly traded company that sells tools for monitoring how software runs, known as observability. It didn’t offer a premium above the $3.8 billion valuation set by venture capital investors, the person said, so Upwind decided to stay independent.

Four-year-old Upwind has grown rapidly amid rising AI-driven cybersecurity threats. The startup has been adding $20 million to $30 million in annualized recurring revenue (ARR) each quarter and is projected to end the year at roughly $90 million, according to a person familiar with Upwind’s financials. That means that VCs and Datadog valued the startup at more than 40 times its forecast ARR, a common yardstick for pricing software companies. The high multiple is also well below the 80x ARR fetched by Cyera, another fast-growing cybersecurity startup, according to TechCrunch reporting from earlier this year.

Cybersecurity is poised to be the third big wave of AI software that companies will pay for after AI coding tools and customer support, Theory Ventures general partner Tomasz Tunguz recently wrote in his widely read blog.

By walking away from an acquisition offer, Upwind clearly believes that the company will ultimately be worth more than the $3.8 billion that Datadog was ready to pay for it. However, given how few cybersecurity companies have gone public in recent years, an eventual sale remains the most likely outcome for the startup.

Upwind continues to draw acquisition interest, according to a person familiar with the company.

The startup was founded by Amiram Shachar, who sold his previous company, the cloud spend management startup Spot.io, to NetApp for $450 million. Upwind calls its approach to thwarting threats “runtime” security, which means it alerts and remedies attacks and vulnerabilities in active services in real time.

TechCrunch has reached out to both Upwind and Datadog for comment.
