The cryptocurrency market is breaking the classical rules of financial economics. The industry has faced the biggest challenge in its history: the FBI confirmed that North Korean hackers attacked Binance's infrastructure and withdrew $6.3 billion.

However, instead of a protracted capitulation, this news triggered a paradoxical reaction: prices held, creating a strong bullish precedent.

Against this backdrop, well-known crypto analyst DonAlt, who accurately predicted the historic 700% XRP rally back in 2024, directly cites the Binance hack as the reason for his ultra-bullish sentiment. In his opinion, in the current situation it is "hard to be a bear" precisely because of how the market reacted to the catastrophe.

The situation was promptly stabilized by the actions of the platform itself, which acted proactively and covered 90% of users' lost funds from its own reserves, and by the Treasury Department. As a result, Bitcoin ignored attempts at mass sell-offs and held around $77,935, while XRP settled at $1.2498.

The main indicator for the analyst was the complete absence of panic follow-through selling after the shocking news. DonAlt draws a direct analogy with the events of November 2022, when the industry was going through the collapse of the FTX exchange:

"Last time the market didn't properly sell off after a huge event like this was the FTX collapse. When I saw the lack of follow through then I got giga bullish. And we subsequently went from 16k to 100k. Hard to be bearish here after having been given the same setup yet again"

The expert emphasizes that there are no 100% guarantees in financial markets and classifies the current situation as a game of mathematical probabilities. According to him, when the market prices in colossal negativity but refuses to go down, the odds in the long run are always on the side of buyers.

Still, DonAlt’s argument rests on a single precedent. The FTX analogy worked once, but one case is not a pattern, and the two events differ in important ways. FTX wiped out customer funds for good, while in the Binance case most losses were covered within days.

A market that does not fall on a compensated hack is responding rationally, not necessarily showing hidden strength.

The real test will come in the next few weeks: if prices hold once the news is fully priced in and attention shifts to the stolen funds moving through mixers, the bullish case gets much stronger. If they don’t, the lack of follow-through may turn out to have been only a delay.

The exchange says withdrawals surged after some services resumed but have since slowed, with the outflows representing a fraction of its roughly $171 billion in customer assets.

Binance has recorded $5.8 billion in net outflows over the past 24 hours as customers withdraw funds following the exchange’s record $6.3 billion hack, according to data from DefiLlama.

Binance said it began restoring withdrawals at 6:00 UTC on Sunday. By 3:30 UTC, it had processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals against $1 billion in deposits, resulting in net outflows of $3.6 billion.

Separate data from DefiLlama showed $5.8 billion in net outflows over the preceding 24 hours, as funds continued leaving the exchange after its initial update.

Binance said withdrawals initially surged but have since slowed and are stabilizing. The exchange noted that the outflows represented a small portion of the approximately $171 billion in assets it holds. Cointelegraph reached out to Binance for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

The flows offered an early test of customer confidence following the $6.3 billion hack against Binance, the largest crypto theft on record.

Related: Binance says phase one of withdrawals opens after $6.3B hack

Binance’s latest update at 12:36 UTC shows it enabled withdrawals for tokens across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and XRP Ledger, adding that it will continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases.

Early data shared by Binance shows that the largest share of withdrawals were in USDt (USDT), followed by USDC (USDC) and Bitcoin (BTC).

On Saturday, Binance said it had replaced 90% of the assets lost in the $6.3 billion hack using funds from its corporate treasury, its Secure Asset Fund for Users and its futures insurance fund.

#5261. Solmate Discloses 1.26M SOL Custody Positions and Says It Has No Binance Exposure

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Solmate Infrastructure has published a specific answer to a question facing crypto treasury companies after an exchange security incident: where are the assets held? In an October 30 disclosure, the company said it had no Binance accounts or exposure and identified the custodians holding its reported 1.26 million SOL.

The Form 6-K places those holdings with Kraken, Anchorage Digital or BitGo as of October 29. It is a company statement about custody at a particular time, rather than an independent audit of every position.

A corporate balance sheet can show exposure to a cryptocurrency without explaining the complete operating arrangement behind it. Investors also need to know who controls transactions, how transfers are approved and whether the company can access the assets when it needs them.

A treasury that plans to hold for years still faces shorter-term obligations. It may need cash for operating costs, collateral for financing or flexibility to respond to an unexpected event. Custody arrangements influence how quickly it can meet those needs.

Publishing the names of service providers improves the starting point for that analysis. It does not reveal the allocation among them, every account condition or the extent to which assets may be committed to another activity. Those details require additional disclosures.

During a security event, markets can struggle to distinguish companies directly affected from those sharing only a connection to the same asset class. A precise statement can reduce that uncertainty without making broader claims about the safety of the industry.

Solmate’s accompanying release says its validator infrastructure continued to operate normally. That addresses another part of the business: the systems participating in network operations, as distinct from where the treasury tokens are held.

The distinction is useful because an operating interruption and a custody loss are not interchangeable. A company could experience one without the other. Reporting them separately makes it easier to understand what an incident has actually changed.

Using more than one custodian can reduce dependence on a single operating platform, but it also creates work. A company must reconcile several records, maintain consistent authorization rules and understand the conditions for moving assets between accounts.

A simple example is a treasury policy requiring two approvals for a transfer. That rule must be enforceable wherever assets are held, rather than exist only in an internal document. Differences among service providers can become important when staff change or an urgent transfer is requested.

There is no evidence in this disclosure of a weakness in Solmate’s procedures. The point is that naming several providers is one component of risk management, not a complete description of it. Clear allocation and operational reporting would give shareholders a fuller view.

The number of SOL held is different from the cash value available to shareholders. That value changes with the token’s price and with the company’s wider liabilities, operating costs and financing structure.

A statement that assets are accounted for therefore cannot be translated into a guarantee about equity value. Nor does an unchanged custody position establish that tokens can be sold at a particular price without affecting execution.

Solmate’s filing is useful because it answers a bounded question with named counterparties and a dated balance. Investors assessing the company can combine that information with subsequent financial reports and operating disclosures, keeping asset safekeeping, liquidity and market exposure as separate parts of the analysis.

#5260. Why Didn't Bitcoin Drop More? Binance's CZ Credits FBI

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) credited the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and other US law enforcement agencies with helping prevent a larger drop in the Bitcoin (BTC) price after the massive $6.3 billion security breach at the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance founder CZ commended the timely actions of the FBI, US Secret Service (USSS), and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) amid the massive security breach.

According to CZ's Nov. 1 post on X, US law enforcement agencies (FBI, USSS, IRS and more) helped "a lot" during the incident.

For instance, they helped with tracking and freezing funds.

According to the Binance co-founder, they were able to prevent an even sharper fall in the Bitcoin price.

"Not enough to express our appreciation in a tweet. There are probably a lot of crypto bros not realizing that a lot of 'why bitcoin didn't drop even more?' credits go to them," CZ stated.

This comes after the FBI officially identified North Korean hackers as being behind the record-breaking Binance hack.

According to the FBI's Oct. 31 announcement, North Korea stole more than $6 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from the Binance crypto exchange on or about Oct. 29.

More specifically, the FBI identified the North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor as being behind the massive cryptocurrency theft.

It's a known North Korean hacker group that has stolen large amounts of cryptocurrencies before.

The FBI noted that investigators, together with the Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, have tracked how the hackers were exchanging stolen cryptocurrencies mainly for Ethereum (ETH).

The FBI warned that these assets could be further laundered using decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The US authorities have called on cryptocurrency businesses and infrastructure providers to block transactions related to the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to stop them from laundering these assets.

Specifically, the US authorities urged THORNode operators, remote procedure call (RPC) node operators, instant exchanges, blockchain analytics companies, DeFi platforms, etc., to block such transactions.

Apart from that, the FBI provided a list of the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to allow other members of the cryptocurrency industry to detect and block suspicious transactions.

The Binance security breach sent shock waves throughout the cryptocurrency market.

Bitcoin tumbled below $77,000 after the market reacted to the unprecedented crypto theft.

BTC dropped to around $76,000 at one point, registering its lowest price in several weeks.

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies like Ethereum, XRP, Solana (SOL), and BNB nosedived as the market reacted to the breach.

Fortunately, Bitcoin eventually found stability and was trading around $78,000 during the early Nov. 1 trading session.

#5259. Hashdex Adds Jane Street to Crypto Index ETF Authorized Participants

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Hashdex Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF has added Jane Street Capital to its list of authorized participants, according to an October 30 prospectus supplement. The document updates the firms able to participate in the product’s creation-and-redemption arrangements.

It is a market-structure development rather than a statement that Jane Street has made a long-term investment in the fund. That distinction matters when institutional names become attached to crypto products.

The SEC’s investor glossary describes authorized participants as financial institutions that enter contractual arrangements to buy and redeem creation units. Their role links the supply of a fund’s shares to activity in the market where those shares trade.

Most ordinary investors transact with another market participant through a brokerage account. An authorized participant operates at a different layer, dealing with larger blocks under the product’s documented procedures. The two activities support the same product but should not be confused.

A listed participant can make the infrastructure available without committing to create shares on every trading day. The appointment establishes a relationship and a permitted function. Actual activity depends on market conditions, commercial decisions and the rules governing the fund.

When demand for shares changes, the mechanisms for adjusting supply can influence how closely the traded price stays connected to underlying asset value. If those mechanisms are difficult or expensive to use, gaps can persist even when traders recognize them.

An additional participant may offer another route through which the market can respond. That can be useful if existing firms face their own balance-sheet constraints or operational interruptions. It does not guarantee narrower spreads, because execution also depends on the liquidity of the assets and the cost of hedging.

Consider a period when investors want to buy shares rapidly while underlying crypto markets are moving. A firm providing liquidity has to manage the price risk between the share transaction and the corresponding asset trade. Access to a creation process is necessary for some workflows, but it does not make that exposure disappear.

The Hashdex supplement also identifies an affiliation between Jane Street Capital and a crypto trading counterparty. Such disclosures help readers understand how firms involved in different parts of the process are connected.

The relevant analytical question is whether the structure can process orders reliably and on competitive terms. An institutional service relationship is not evidence that the firm expects the underlying cryptocurrencies to rise or that it will retain a directional position.

This is particularly important when reading fund-flow headlines. Net new shares, secondary-market turnover and an authorized-participant appointment describe different things. One concerns changes in product size, another concerns trading between holders, and the third concerns the operating network behind the product.

Useful follow-up measures include trading spreads, premiums or discounts and the consistency of creation and redemption activity. Those observations would show whether the expanded network changes the experience for investors.

They also need context. A wider spread during an unusually volatile session does not automatically establish that the fund’s structure has failed. Comparing conditions over time and against underlying-market liquidity is more informative than judging a single quote.

The October filing is a relatively small document with a meaningful operational purpose: it updates who can help connect the fund to its underlying markets. It adds a recognizable financial firm to that machinery, while leaving the investment case and future flow direction open to separate assessment.

A headline claiming that 1.8 billion XRP moved across the XRP Ledger within 24 hours has revived discussion of a network recovery. The figure hasn't been independently verified for a dated 24-hour period, so treat it as a reported claim, not confirmed evidence of a new trend.

The XRP Ledger handles payments, decentralized exchange transactions and tokenized assets. Payment volumes reflects the network activity, but the number needs context. None of that necessarily signals fresh investor demand or new capital entering the market.

Recent verified reporting shows why the distinction matters. One October snapshot had daily payment volume jumping to about 137.7 million XRP, still below its 30-day average of roughly 496 million.

Another October reading, around 363.3 million XRP, came with the same caution: a one-day rise did not establish a sustained recovery.

A reading near 1.8 billion XRP usually comes at the end of the week where most of the network activity occurs. The most likely outcome is always the same: high activity by Thursday and Friday and a tubmling on the weekend, with a recovery starting on Monday.

Other indicators help separate real adoption from a passing spike: active addresses, successful payment counts, decentralized-exchange trading, liquidity and how transaction sizes are distributed. Even high transaction counts can mislead when automated activity dominates, as recent investigations into small-value stablecoin payments on XRPL showed.

Network usage and XRP's market price are only indirectly related. More settlement activity doesn't guarantee higher token prices, and speculative buying can lift prices with no matching improvement in usage. Broader market conditions and exchange liquidity matter too.

A verified natural burst of XRP movement could mean renewed engagement with the network. A more convincing signal would be several consecutive days of stronger, widely distributed activity, backed by improving liquidity and sustained user demand, which rarely happens.

#5256. Chrome Can Now Pull Details From Your Gmail to Fill Out Web Forms

Chrome Can Now Pull Details From Your Gmail to Fill Out Web Forms

Google’s Chrome browser can now pull personal details from your Gmail inbox to fill out online forms for you, the company said in its announcement on Wednesday.

The update, called “enhanced autofill,” suggests order numbers, tracking information, and flight bookings when a form asks for them, wrote Amanda Lim, a Chrome product manager, in the announcement. Autofill is the browser tool that types in details like your name and address so you don’t have to.

It runs on Gemini, Google’s AI assistant, through a feature called Personal Intelligence, which lets Gemini draw on connected apps such as Gmail and Google Photos to tailor its answers to your own life. It is rolling out to Gemini in Chrome users who have Personal Intelligence turned on, on desktop, Android and iOS, starting in the U.S.

Google’s post names only those three kinds of data as coming from Gmail. Credit card numbers and addresses are part of Chrome’s standard autofill, which fills them from details you have saved in the browser, and the announcement does not say the new feature pulls them out of your inbox.

“You can manage whether enhanced autofill is enabled and what it can access via your Chrome settings,” Lim wrote. “As always, sensitive data is encrypted and you remain in control.”

Encryption scrambles data so only Google and other authorized parties can read it, though the post does not explain how that applies to the Gmail content Chrome reads or what it scans.

Users choose whether to connect their apps and can switch the connections off at any time, the post says, though Google does train on limited information, such as specific prompts and the model’s responses.

In November, users pushed back on a Smart Features setting that let Gemini analyze emails and calendars unless they opted out, and Google said it had not changed its underlying data-handling practices.

Chrome also dropped a line from its settings saying on-device AI, meaning models that run on your own computer rather than Google’s servers, works without sending data to Google servers. Google said the wording change did not reflect a change in how it handles on-device AI.

The rollout began Wednesday in the U.S. on desktop, Android and iOS, and Google’s announcement gives no date for other countries

#5255. WalletConnect Adds Stellar Payments as Bermuda Ticketing Rollout Targets 2027

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

WalletConnect is expanding payment access on Stellar while preparing a separate merchant rollout in Bermuda. Its October 29 announcement says WalletConnect Pay supports the network, with LOBSTR as the first live Stellar wallet.

The Bermuda initiative, developed with Penrose Partners, begins with ticketing platform Premier Tickets, or PTIX. That integration is expected in the second quarter of 2027, so wallet support available now should be distinguished from the planned merchant launch.

A payment interface needs to identify both the customer’s wallet and the transaction the merchant expects. Those tasks sound simple until an order expires, a customer changes devices or a transfer arrives after the checkout page has been closed.

For ticketing, the sequence is particularly important. The buyer wants confirmation that a seat has been secured; the organizer needs confidence that payment belongs to the correct order. A blockchain transaction hash does not, by itself, contain every detail of that commercial relationship.

A useful integration must connect payment status to inventory and customer support. Otherwise, a fast transfer can still create a slow service experience when the ticketing system cannot confidently match the money to the purchase.

The proposed PTIX arrangement sends customer funds to the event organizer’s wallet without the ticketing platform holding them. That design changes where money sits between the moment a customer pays and the moment the organizer can use it.

It can reduce the need for the platform to collect and subsequently distribute balances. It also requires careful handling of refunds, disputed orders and changes to an event. Those obligations do not disappear because the transfer takes a more direct route.

A cancelled concert offers a straightforward example. Returning a payment requires identifying the right recipient, confirming the amount and deciding which party is responsible for making the transfer. A well-designed service should make that process comprehensible to a customer who has no interest in the underlying network.

For an organizer, receiving a digital asset is useful only if it fits the business’s finances. The organizer needs to know how much usable value it has received, what costs apply and how the balance will pay suppliers or other expenses.

Some businesses may want to retain a token; others may prefer conversion into bank money. Those choices affect reconciliation and liquidity planning. The availability of a wallet connection does not establish that every merchant will make the same decision.

Payment records also need to remain useful after the event. A business must be able to connect sales, refunds and settlement to its own accounts. The more the system can handle these ordinary tasks predictably, the less specialist knowledge a merchant needs to accept the payment method.

The announced timeline gives observers a clear milestone: a functioning ticket purchase from a supported wallet, with a merchant receiving the expected funds and a buyer receiving the correct ticket. That is a more useful measure than the theoretical reach of a wallet network.

After launch, repeat use and the rate of failed or abandoned payments would help assess whether the option solves a real customer problem. Lower processing costs would matter if they survive the full journey, including conversion and support.

WalletConnect’s Stellar expansion opens a technical route, while the Bermuda project attempts to give that route a regular commercial purpose. The two developments fit together, but their different launch stages need to remain clear as the integration progresses.

#5254. THORChain halts swaps after block reorg bug, slowing Binance hackers

THORChain node operators paused swaps involving assets on 10 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron.

THORChain halted swaps across multiple blockchains on Saturday after an Ethereum block reorganization exposed a refund bug, which may have inadvertently slowed the movement of funds stolen from Binance, according to Chainalysis.

According to THORChain, the incident began at 11:34 UTC on Saturday, when a one-block reorganization on Ethereum removed a 10 ETH deposit that THORChain had already credited. When the swap failed to meet its price limit, THORChain issued a refund against funds the vault had never received. The sender’s actual deposit was also refunded, resulting in an extra 10 ETH payout, which then triggered an automatic pause.

An Ethereum block reorganization, or reorg, happens when the network replaces a recent block with a competing block. The newly discovered flaw lets THORChain refund a payment that Ethereum no longer recognizes as having happened. A malicious actor could potentially exploit that mismatch.

“Now that this is public knowledge, every time there is a block re-org on an external chain, a malicious actor could perform a new transaction with the same nonce and would be paid funds by the THORChain vaults,” the protocol’s team said.

THORChain node operators paused swaps involving assets on 10 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron, while trading continued on Avalanche, Base and XRP, according to the protocol’s network status page.

“Nodes will decide to re-enable chains as they are deemed safe,” said THORChain.

The trading halt also disrupted attempts by North Korean hackers to launder funds stolen in last week’s $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Chainalysis.

“THORChain just inadvertently delayed the laundering of a significant amount of funds stolen from Binance,” said Chainalysis on Sunday, explaining the emergency pause is “preventing all users, including DPRK’s money launderers, from using cross-chain swaps.”

“Until the service comes back online, neither the hackers nor anyone else can swap through a majority of THORChain’s bridges,” said Chainalysis.

The disruption came as US authorities pressed crypto infrastructure providers to restrict the movement of stolen funds.

On Saturday, the FBI urged THORChain node operators, DeFi services and other virtual asset providers to block transactions associated with addresses used by TraderTraitor to launder proceeds from the Binance hack.

Related: THORChain’s RUNE jumps 13% after Binance’s record $6.3B hack

North Korean hackers have used THORChain to permissionlessly swap cryptocurrencies following previous attacks.

However, THORChain has continued to defend its role as neutral, permissionless infrastructure amid scrutiny over stolen funds moving through the protocol.

In its third-quarter report, the project said it maintained that position despite pressure to block transactions linked to hacked funds.

THORChain founder John-Paul Thorbjornsen separately defended the protocol’s commitment to permissionless transactions, warning against shutting it down in response to pressure over illicit funds.

“IMO if THORNodes decided to take the protocol offline next week then the experiment is over,” he said.

“The last bastion of unencumbered and neutral settlement is over. There will simply be no other venue and the protocol would have failed.”

In late October 2026, Zcash (ZEC) reached a key milestone: the coin's price consolidated around $1,280, and its market capitalization hit $21.8 billion. However, the rapid rally was overshadowed by a sharp split within the community.

The trigger of the crisis was not a technical problem but a revolt of large investors over the targeted spending of capital.

Zcash Community Grants (ZCG), the organization that distributes part of the miners' block reward, launched the Zcash Adoption Pool program. The fund directed grants toward the integration of vulnerable groups like refugees without access to banks.

The decision sparked protest from major players, since ZCG's charter allows it to distribute multimillion-dollar budgets bypassing the coinholder vote. The "whale" revolt moved into the practical realm: a major holder under the pseudonym "big z" publicly announced a full sell-off of his ZEC holdings.

According to him, the fund should finance cryptography, not political manifestos.

The local conflict quickly grew into a debate about the nature of decentralized money, which industry heavyweights joined. Developer Sean Bowe published a manifesto on the future of ZCG, in which he called for revising the fund's financing due to the anomalous surge in the ZEC price.

The initiative was unexpectedly supported by legendary investor Naval Ravikant, who laconically snapped that a $50 million cap is more than enough for community grants.

Meanwhile, the fund's activists continue to insist that private money is a "humanitarian imperative" and a public good.

However, Gemini exchange co-founder Tyler Winklevoss harshly challenged this thesis: a commercial network with transaction fees cannot be a public good. Winklevoss compared ZCG's actions to "taxation without representation" and called for leaving the development of Zcash to the free market.

The pressure on the price from the whales' coin sell-off coincided with the launch of direct ZEC deposits on the decentralized Rujira Network on October 29.

After failing to break above $1,390, the price settled in the $1,220–1,245 $range, still well below the all-time high of $1,698 set in late September. The fundamental dispute over who should control Zcash's millions remains open.

#5251. Airtm and BVNK Plan Wallet Payments for Merchants in Emerging Markets

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Airtm and BVNK have announced an integration intended to let users spend wallet funds with participating retailers, extending digital-dollar services beyond receiving and holding money. The October 29 joint announcement links Airtm Connect with BVNK’s stablecoin-payment infrastructure and says the integration will use Stellar.

The commercial objective is straightforward: a balance becomes more useful if its owner can spend it without repeatedly moving through disconnected services. Delivering that convenience requires the entire payment process to work, including the steps outside the blockchain.

A customer who receives digital dollars may still need to pay merchants using a different system. Each conversion or transfer can introduce a fee, a delay and another opportunity to select the wrong details.

Connecting a wallet directly to a merchant payment flow could remove some of that handling. The user would begin with the balance they already possess, rather than first preparing money in a separate account solely for the purchase.

The improvement depends on whether the customer can understand the final cost before confirming. A low network fee is only one element. Exchange rates, payment-provider charges and any conversion into the merchant’s chosen settlement currency also determine what the purchase actually costs.

A payment option is difficult to use regularly if adding money to the wallet is unreliable. Conversely, convenient funding has limited value if the customer cannot use the resulting balance where they shop.

The partnership combines providers working at different parts of that chain. The implication is a chance to make funding, wallet access and merchant acceptance feel like one service, even when multiple organizations perform the underlying work.

Consider someone paid by an overseas customer who then purchases a subscription. A coherent flow should preserve enough information to show the incoming payment, the available balance, the purchase and any refund. If the customer must reconstruct those records across several interfaces, some of the convenience has been lost.

A successful network transaction and a completed retail order are related, but they are not identical. The merchant needs to know that the transfer corresponds to a valid order and meets its settlement requirements before delivering the product.

That creates several possible intermediate states. A customer may approve a payment after the original quote expires. A merchant may cancel an order while a transfer is processing. A service may need to reverse the commercial transaction even though the blockchain transfer itself cannot simply be deleted.

These are normal payment-system problems rather than reasons to dismiss the model. The quality of an integration shows in how consistently it handles them, especially for users who cannot afford to wait through a lengthy support process to recover a modest balance.

The announcement establishes a planned route to participating retailers. It does not imply that every merchant connected to a broader financial network will immediately accept an Airtm wallet payment.

Practical evidence would include which countries and merchants are enabled, the available funding methods and the time between payment approval and a usable settlement balance. Successful repeat purchases would say more about adoption than the number of people who could theoretically access the service.

For stablecoin markets, this is a useful test of whether digital-dollar infrastructure can support ordinary spending without adding complexity for the customer. Airtm and BVNK have described the connection they want to build. Its value will come from how well funding, checkout and after-sales support fit together once people use it.

According to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, the Binance hacker has dumped more than 130 altcoins across EVM chains, generating about $279 million in proceeds.

A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance last Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Binance's initial investigation suggested the security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

How many altcoins has the Binance hacker dumped? On EVM chains alone, the hacker dumped over 130 altcoins, receiving: 123,400 $ETH ($277.26M) 1.69M $USDC Total: $279M https://t.co/Y8JYpWRP73

In a recent analysis on X, Lookonchain examined how many altcoins the Binance hacker has dumped. It noted that on EVM chains alone, the hacker dumped over 130 altcoins, sharing the list of some tokens affected in a table including SHIB. The hacker dumped 499,926,072,560 SHIB with a selling value of 873 ETH worth $1,960,615.

In return for the altcoins sold, the hacker received 123,400 ETH worth $277.26 million and 1.69 million USDC, totaling approximately $279 million.

The Binance hacker continues to swap stolen funds. In a recent report by Lookonchain, the hacker is swapping the stolen 970,522 SOL worth $95.9 million for BTC.

As reported, the over 499 billion SHIB stolen in the Binance hack represented 0.05% of its supply, with the SHIB price relatively absorbing the selloff.

Shiba Inu price saw a sharp selloff on October 29, alongside the rest of the crypto market in an initial reaction to the news of the Binance hack. The drop hit a low of $0.00000446 on Friday, from where SHIB sharply rebounded. Shiba Inu closed Saturday in the red, marking a loss of 18.92% in October.

Shiba Inu rebounded thereafter, fluctuating between $0.00000466 and $0.00000472 on November's first day as the price awaits further direction. At the time of writing, SHIB was down 0.04% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000469 and down 3.14% weekly.

Binance says it has replenished about 95% of the impacted assets, reiterating a clear commitment to absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds. The crypto exchange also said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.

#5249. Taurus Adds Stellar Smart-Contract Assets to Institutional Custody and Issuance

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Taurus has expanded its Stellar integration to support smart-contract-based assets, giving institutional clients a broader set of custody and issuance functions. The company said on October 29 that the capabilities are live through Taurus-PROTECT and Taurus-CAPITAL.

The official announcement describes an extension of existing Stellar support rather than a newly announced fund or security. The change matters because institutions need more than a place to store a token once it has been created.

Safekeeping is often described as protecting private keys. For an institution, a useful custody system must also govern what those keys are allowed to authorize, who can request an action and which approvals are needed before it proceeds.

A simple transfer and a smart-contract interaction can carry different consequences. An instruction may change an allowance, invoke a contract function or alter how an asset can be handled. The approving person needs enough information to understand that consequence before a signature is produced.

This creates a practical reason to integrate smart-contract support into the tools an institution already uses. A separate experimental interface may be technically capable of sending an instruction while sitting outside the organization’s normal operating controls.

Creating a tokenized instrument requires decisions about the rights it represents and the actions permitted after issuance. Depending on the instrument, those may include transfers, subscriptions, redemptions or changes governed by the issuer’s rules.

Taurus says the release supports several Stellar token models, including structures intended for regulated assets. That flexibility can help an institution match its technical implementation to the instrument it wants to offer, rather than treating every token as economically identical.

It also raises an integration question: can the legal and operational records remain consistent with the contract state? A token should not appear transferable in an application when the issuer’s rules prohibit the intended recipient from holding it.

A financial firm considering another blockchain faces costs beyond deploying a contract. Staff need familiar approval processes, finance teams need reports and operations teams need a procedure for handling failed instructions.

Reusing an established custody and issuance interface may reduce the number of new systems those teams must learn. It can also make oversight more consistent across networks, provided the interface still exposes the differences that matter.

For example, an operations dashboard should not imply that two assets have identical settlement behaviour simply because they appear in neighbouring rows. Network-specific requirements, contract permissions and servicing obligations need to remain visible where they affect decisions.

The release establishes that clients have more infrastructure options on Stellar. The next evidence of adoption would be institutions using those capabilities for named instruments with clearly explained ownership and transfer arrangements.

There is a difference between supporting a contract standard and completing a reliable asset-servicing process. A production service must handle routine transactions, unusual requests and the reconciliation that follows. Its value lies in reducing the effort required to do those jobs correctly.

For Stellar, the potential benefit is a wider route for institutional asset activity. For Taurus clients, it is the ability to consider another network without rebuilding every surrounding control. Neither outcome should be measured simply by the number of token standards listed in a release.

The more revealing test is whether an issuer can take an asset from creation through ongoing management and eventual redemption using a coherent set of records. Taurus’s announcement expands the available toolkit for that work; actual products and operating results will show how effectively it is used.

#5248. Can TRON reclaim $0.33 after its $234M hack fueled buying spree?

On Thursday, the 29th of October, TRON [TRX] prices surged from $0.328 to $0.365 in a matter of hours. Attackers who had drained Binance hot wallets for $6.3 billion across ten blockchains rushed to swap their USDT for TRX.

Since Tether can freeze its stablecoin, the urgency to swap to TRX, where no central issuer can block transfers, saw a $234 million USDT swap to TRX on SunSwap, at $0.367 per TRX, blockchain data firm Bitquery confirmed.

At that time, the TRX market price had been only $0.33, which helped explain the swift price surge. Other intelligence platforms have since reported whale wallets with the stolen funds, turning the artificial buying spree into a supply overhang for the global stablecoin settlement giant.

Since Thursday’s price spike, the Layer 1 blockchain’s native token has witnessed a 13.4% price correction. Incidentally, the market structure on the 1-day timeframe had been bearish.

The swing move southward from $0.3775 to $0.3108 in May and early June was the one that dictated the bearish market structure. Using these levels, Fibonacci retracement levels were plotted.

The 78.6% Fibonacci retracement level was at $0.363, and the price surge halted just above this level on Thursday. Thereafter, a daily session close below $0.3108 ensued.

The OBV was sliding lower, continuing the downtrend of recent weeks, while the MACD also took a sharp nosedive.

The MACD formed a bullish crossover in bearish territory, signaling a price bounce was underway. Based on the size of the impulse move down from $0.365, it is likely that the current bounce could go to $0.333-$0.352.

On the way, the $0.33 supply zone was also a place that could see a bearish price reaction.

Swing traders and long-term investors need to be mindful of the larger bear trend at play. A price bounce to $0.33 followed by a slide toward $0.30 or even $0.27 is a possibility for TRX in the coming weeks.

October ended for XRP with a drop of almost 19%. The main blow was the $6.3 billion hack of the Binance exchange, which dragged down the entire market. However, the sell-off recorded at the lows activated large buy orders — the current liquidity map points to the formation of local support.

Now the XRP price is squeezed in a narrow corridor around $1.25, testing the boundaries of the local bottom.

CoinGlass derivatives market data shows that the asset has literally been pinned to the floor. At the current rate of $1.2505, the critical level of long liquidations is at the $1.2292 mark. The probability of its test within 24 hours is 54%. From above, the price is held back by a block of short sellers at the $1.4292 level.

At the same time, the market has already been cleared of excessive leverage — $37.6 million in longs were forcibly closed in October.

The TradingView technical picture confirms the importance of the current line. The daily oscillator dropped to the 36.85 mark.

Historically, reaching this oversold zone has always preceded an upward trend reversal.

Additional pressure was exerted by the results of the Ripple Swell conference. The new RLUSD stablecoin takes over the company’s institutional products (including custodial services for Coinbase and Robinhood), which temporarily reduced direct demand for XRP.

Conversely, a breakdown of $1.20 will open the way to the August lows around $0.98–$1.00.

#5246. Coinbase Swings to $719 Million Q3 Profit on Crypto Gains

Coinbase Swings to $719 Million Q3 Profit on Crypto Gains

Coinbase is back in the black, though much of that came from the crypto on its own balance sheet.

The exchange reported third-quarter net income of $719 million, or $2.51 per diluted share, on Thursday, ending a two-quarter losing streak. Analysts had expected a loss of 15 cents per share, according to Zacks. But about $715 million of the profit came from gains on crypto Coinbase holds as an investment. Excluding those and other investment gains, adjusted net income was $78 million.

Total revenue came in at $1.22 billion, in line with expectations, flat from the second quarter and down 35% from a year earlier. Transaction revenue slipped 1% to $590 million but beat the roughly $527 million analysts expected, as crypto volatility sank to multiyear lows and trading volume across the market fell.

The standout was prediction markets, which crossed $200 million in annualized revenue, making it one of the fastest-growing products in Coinbase’s history, the company said.

Daily traders grew more than 60% from the prior quarter, and revenue has compounded 82% per quarter since launch. CEO Brian Armstrong said the product kept “growing even through slower sports months.”

“Prediction markets are adding another revenue stream and are less correlated to crypto volatility,” CFO Alesia Haas said.

Coinbase also cut its 2026 adjusted expense guidance by another $100 million at the midpoint, to between $4.15 billion and $4.3 billion, following cost reductions in May. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 60% from the prior quarter to $333 million. Through Oct. 25, fourth-quarter transaction revenue stood at about $165 million.

The positive results follow two consecutive losing quarters. Coinbase posted a $394 million loss in the first quarter and missed estimates in the second as trading activity slowed, though analysts said at the time they weren’t worried about the stock’s slide.

Shares closed Thursday at $160.59, down 1.1%, before the results came out, and were little changed in after-hours trading. The stock is down more than 55% from its 52-week high of $361.40.

#5245. Ripple and Water.org Expand Stablecoin Work as Aid Payments Move Faster

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Ripple and Water.org are expanding a partnership that applies payment and stablecoin infrastructure to water and sanitation financing. Ripple’s late-October announcement describes wider use of Ripple Payments, RLUSD and wallet services across the nonprofit’s operations.

The company reports that earlier work moved more than $3.2 million across four markets, with same-day settlement in Mexico and Brazil replacing waits of two to three days. Those are partner-reported operational results, not an independent measure of every programme outcome.

Water.org’s WaterCredit programme works with local financial institutions to make small loans for household water and sanitation improvements. Its role includes supporting partners with resources and expertise, while those institutions provide the financing.

That model makes the movement of capital an important operational link. Money may originate in one country, pass through an international funding arrangement and ultimately support a local loan used to install a tap, toilet or other improvement.

Speed in one part of that chain can help, particularly when it reduces idle balances or uncertainty over when funds will arrive. It cannot substitute for sound lending, reliable local contractors or a household’s ability to use the completed infrastructure.

A cross-border transfer can involve several forms of cost: bank charges, currency conversion, the time staff spend reconciling records and the cash held while a payment is pending. A change in infrastructure may improve some of those elements without changing all of them.

The useful comparison is therefore the amount and timing of usable money at the destination. A token arriving quickly is not the same as a local lender having the currency and information needed to disburse a loan.

For example, a settlement message that arrives over a weekend may still require a local conversion or approval process. Measuring that whole sequence would show whether continuous digital settlement translates into a practical advantage for the programme.

Adding a stablecoin gives an organization another way to hold and transfer a claim denominated in dollars. It also creates tasks around access permissions, reconciliation and the conditions for converting the balance into another form of money.

A nonprofit’s finance team needs to connect those balances to grants, programme budgets and expenditure records. The technology is most useful when it fits that discipline, rather than requiring the organization to maintain a separate set of unexplained onchain transactions.

Custody and wallet services can form part of that operating model. The important question is who is allowed to move funds and how the organization checks that an instruction matches an approved purpose. Faster settlement increases the value of getting those controls right before execution.

Payment completion times and processing costs show whether the financial infrastructure works more efficiently. Household access to safe water and sanitation shows whether the wider programme achieves its purpose. Both are relevant, but one should not be used as an automatic proxy for the other.

A credible expansion would report the relationship between the two: whether lower costs leave more funding available, whether quicker transfers improve loan availability and whether local delivery remains reliable as the programme grows.

For crypto, this is an adoption story with a concrete use for moving money, rather than a claim that a token’s price must benefit. The partnership gives Ripple and Water.org a setting in which payment infrastructure can be assessed against a practical objective. The strongest results will be those that trace an operational improvement through to the people the financing is intended to reach.
